title: The world, close
hookLine: the Zen ox-herding pictures don't end on the mountain or in the empty circle: the herder walks back into the market with helping hands
tomorrow: one arrow hits. where does the second one come from?

cards: A crowded hallway, a loud group chat, a tense meeting. Some days the dream is a cabin far from all of it. Zen has a set of pictures about that dream: the ten ox-herding pictures.
A herder has lost his ox, which Zen teachers read as his own true nature. He follows the tracks. He glimpses it, catches it, tames it, and rides it home playing a flute.
Then the ox is gone, then the herder too: an empty circle. That sounds like the end.

teach.h: THE RIVER FLOWS, THE FLOWERS ARE RED.
teach.b: It isn't. After the empty circle comes a picture of the plain world: the river flowing on, the flowers simply red. And then the last picture.
Barefoot, chest bare, a gourd at his side, mixing with people in the market.
The title says he enters the city with bliss-bestowing hands. The verse beside it says that, without any magic powers, he makes withered trees bloom.
That's the Zen teaching the series lands on: awakening isn't finished on the mountain or in the silence. It's finished in the marketplace, among ordinary people, helping.
In the pictures, practice doesn't lift the herder out of the world. It brings him back into it, lighter, with open hands. Not preaching at anyone.
And notice who he is by then: nobody special to look at. A cheerful man in the crowd, the kind of neighbor whose name you learn.

how: Zen teachers use the ten ox-herding pictures, with their short verses, to describe the stages of practice. The last picture, returning to the marketplace, is read as practice lived among ordinary people.

o: the planet as seen from space
ordinary life, entered with helping hands
a place to escape from as fast as you can

s: the ox-herding pictures end with the herder alone on a mountain
they end in the marketplace, among people, with helping hands.
after the empty circle, the pictures return to ordinary nature
the ninth shows the plain world: the river flowing, the flowers red.
in Zen, leaving the world behind is the final goal
in the tenth picture, the herder walks back into town.

games.q: a friend back from a month-long meditation retreat says everyday people now feel shallow to her. what does the tenth ox picture suggest?
o: bring what she found back into ordinary life, among people
move to the retreat for good, since that's the real goal
keep her practice private and stay away from crowds
games.why: the pictures don't stop at the mountain or the empty circle. the herder returns to the market, ordinary and useful.

practice: Take a pen and write down one change from these two weeks in the world: a name you learned, a reply you didn't send, a share you gave. One line is enough.
Then rest your hands open on your knees, the way the herder walks into town, until the sit is done.

wordCard.voice: The world: in Zen's last ox-herding picture, the marketplace, where the herder comes back with open, helping hands.

orig.note: Chinese: the ten ox pictures, a Zen series of images and short verses.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: in the world, back in the market with open hands. That closes two weeks out here; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, with verses attributed to Kuoan Shiyuan (the search, the tracks, seeing, catching, taming, riding home, the ox forgotten, the empty circle, returning to the source, entering the city with bliss-bestowing hands)
